transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-04
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mike Chen (HaloOps CTO), Lina Alvarez (Head of Platform), Derek Holt (SRE)

Auto-generated summary (may be rough):
Jordan: quick onboarding and goals - sizing reserved GPU pools, understanding isolation and KMS, planning a small sim/POC to validate burst coverage and fallback latency.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: Alright everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood — AE on the account. With me is Priya, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Mike: Good, thanks. Busy week but excited to get this scoped.
[00:12] Lina: Hi. We wanted to run through whether dedicated reserved GPUs makes sense for HaloOps given some upcoming regulatory work and spikes from our mobile pipeline.
[00:21] Priya: Perfect. High level, we'll cover three things: sizing (how many nodes / GPUs), isolation requirements (VPC, KMS, audit logs), and burst strategy (warm pools, pre-warm, fallback to hosted). Then propose a small sim POC.
[00:35] Derek: Quick callout — we saw a big spike last month during a campaign, peak TPS went from 120 to 680 for like 10 minutes, so cost concerns are real.
[00:45] Jordan: Good data point. That spike is exactly what reserved + warm pool is supposed to help with. Before we dig in, Lina, can you give us a quick overview of current infra and where inference runs today?
[00:56] Lina: Sure. Right now it's mostly hosted endpoints — CloudAI for models and some self-hosted lama2 on prem for sensitive workloads. The hosted endpoints are fine for baseline but we need lower p95 and guaranteed isolation for certain customers. We also have an internal KMS (Hashicorp Vault) in our VPC.
[01:12] Priya: Got it. So two drivers: latency/SLA and data residency/isolation. For dedicated we can offer VPC peering and customer-managed KMS via Redwood Private path or dedicated with KMS integration. Small note — sometimes our auto transcr has K V cash instead of KV cache, ignore that.
[01:30] Mike: Ha, thanks. On the SLA side, what are realistic p95 numbers we can expect on dedicated vs hosted? We're targeting 150ms for p95 on text-generation for our primary model.
[01:41] Priya: Typical p95 on dedicated for similar models is 60–120ms depending on sequence length, batching behavior, and model quant. Hosted can also hit low latencies but with noisy neighbors your tail may be higher. With dedicated reserved GPUs and warm pools, consistent 100–150ms p95 is doable.
[02:00] Jordan: We should also mention fallback — if you want absolute uptime we can route overflow to hosted variants or scaled-down models with a policy. That keeps the app online but with slightly different quality.
[02:10] Derek: How does cost break down? If we reserve capacity for peaks that run 10 minutes/day, we're worried about paying for mostly idle GPUs.
[02:18] Jordan: Totally. That's why we propose three scenarios: conservative, balanced, and aggressive. Each pairs a reserved baseline with a warm pool and a configurable burst floor that can spill to hosted. Pricing will show reserved monthly cost vs expected monthly token costs on hosted.
[02:33] Mike: We'll need to see the numbers. Also regulatory folks will ask about audit logs of usage and what data touches Redwood.
[02:40] Priya: We log per-request metadata and offer audit exports; for Private we can run the control plane in your VPC (air-gapped option exists) and KMS integrated so keys never leave your environment. SOC2 details are in the security brief; we'll share that.
[02:54] Lina: Can you walk through how isolation works? Specifically tenant fencing and hot pool pre-warm — what does 'isolation' mean at node level?
[03:03] Priya: Sure. Dedicated reserved pools give you topology controls: node-level tenancy (single-tenant) or grouped tenancy (segregated tenants on isolated GPUs). Warm pools are pre-warmed containers/instances that keep KV cache primed for particular models. That reduces cold-starts. We also provide network isolation via VPC peering and private endpoints, and KMS integration for in-flight encryption keys.
[03:24] Derek: You said KV cache — I saw in the docs something about prefix caching and token reuse. How are keys managed when we do customer KMS?
[03:32] Priya: With customer KMS the encryption keys are in your Vault/HSM. Redwood stores ciphertext; we never have plaintext keys. There are operational hooks for rotation and audit. I should note sometimes the cadence of pre-warm and cache priming depends on model session patterns.
[03:48] Mike: For the burst sim POC, what inputs do you need from us? We can get telemetry but how granular should it be?
[03:55] Jordan: Ideally: 7 days of request timestamps, payload sizes, model type mapping, and p95/p99 latencies for each route. That lets us simulate realistic QPS distribution and craft a warm-pool sizing plan.
[04:08] Lina: We can do that. We'll pull logs from last week and last high-traffic day.
[04:13] Priya: For the simulation we also need an idea of model weights — e.g., heavy token-generation routes vs embeddings. If some routes are short sequences we can use tighter batch windows.
[04:24] Derek: Any difference between choosing Redwood Dedicated (reserved) vs Redwood Private on-prem for us?
[04:29] Priya: Private (VPC/on-prem) is for strict data residency or air-gapped regulatory needs. It gives you the most control but has higher setup and maintenance. Dedicated reserved (hosted but isolated) gives a middle ground: we reserve physical GPU capacity for you with tenancy controls and VPC networking while we manage the infra.
[04:46] Mike: On the failover story, if reserved pool saturates and we spill to hosted, what's the expected impact on latency and model fidelity?
[04:53] Jordan: Two choices: 1) Spill to same model on hosted — similar fidelity, slightly higher p95; 2) Spill to smaller/quantized variant — lower latency but possibly lower quality. You define policy per route.
[05:06] Mike: Sounds reasonable. For compliance we need retention windows for logs and proof-of-encryption. Can you give a sample of the audit export?
[05:13] Priya: Yes, we'll attach a sample CSV/JSON audit export in the follow-ups. It includes request id, timestamp, route, model id, bytes in/out, and a KMS key footprint (ciphertext refs).
[05:25] Derek: Regarding pre-warm cost — do warm pools count as reserved GPUs or are they separate billable units?
[05:31] Jordan: Warm pools are part of the reserved strategy — you can configure how many pre-warmed slots are kept. They are reserved capacity so included in the committed cost, but we show amortized unit cost vs cold-start token spend so you can make the tradeoff.
[05:45] Mike: Ok. Let's talk about the three scenarios you mentioned and what they'd look like for our baseline 200 QPS steady with 10 spikes/day to 600 QPS for 5–15 minutes.
[05:56] Priya: (explains) Conservative: reserve enough GPUs to cover 70% of peak and spill rest to hosted — lowest committed cost. Balanced: reserve to cover typical peak with warm pool sized to cover short spikes — moderate commit. Aggressive: reserve full peak with larger warm pool for zero-spill — highest commit but lowest per-token cost and predictable latency. We'll put concrete GPU counts once we see your telemetry.
[06:22] Lina: How do you model queuing and batching in the sim? Our burst shape is very bursty — lots of tiny requests rather than few big ones.
[06:30] Priya: Our sim models arrival process, request size distribution, and queue/backpressure. We simulate model internals: batch windowing, average token generation time, KV cache hit rates. We sometimes approximate attention compute but it's sufficient for sizing. There is some approximation (we'll note where it's approximate).
[06:48] Mike: Great. Any recommended rollout plan if we decide to go dedicated? We want to minimize risk and avoid long lead times.
[06:54] Jordan: Typical rollout: pilot with one reserved pool for non-critical traffic (2–4 weeks), run sim and soak test, then expand to production routes with canary traffic (A/B) and autoscale rules. Lead times for reserved commits are usually 2–6 weeks depending on region/hardware.
[07:08] Derek: Are there penalties for resizing down after a commit period? We might want seasonal reserve adjustments.
[07:13] Jordan: Commit terms are flexible — monthly/annual. We can tailor a plan for seasonality; there can be a resizing window with prorated adjustments. We'll surface that in pricing scenarios.
[07:24] Lina: Security folks will ask about SSO, RBAC and integration with our IdP.
[07:28] Priya: We support SAML SSO, SCIM for provisioning, and granular RBAC. We'll include a security checklist in the docs we share.
[07:36] Mike: Anything else we should watch for? The legal team may want a data processing addendum for PII handling.
[07:41] Jordan: We'll include DPA and SOC2 artifacts. For PII we recommend tokenization or a private deployment if they insist on full on-prem key control.
[07:50] (brief cross-talk as Jordan and Priya confirm attachments they'll share)
[08:05] Jordan: Ok last: scheduling the POC sim workshop — Priya, we'll need your team for a 90-minute session. Lina, Derek — is the week of 6/15 doable?
[08:15] Lina: Yes, that works. We can assemble telemetry and SRE folks.
[08:19] Derek: Will do. I'll pull logs.
[08:22] Mike: We'll review pricing scenarios once you send them. Expect follow-up from legal on DPA.
[08:28] Jordan: Great — recap/next steps in chat. Thanks everyone.
[08:31] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings: "lama2" was spoken as "lama two"; KV cache sometimes transcribed as K V cash; Redwood Dedicated referred to as Redwood Dedicate once. Natural pauses and crosstalk present.

References shared: Redwood dedicated + private capabilities deck (link: https://redwood.ai/decks/dedicated-capabilities) [note: placeholder], Security brief (link: /shared/security-brief.pdf), Sample audit export (will attach).
